text.p: Russian Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov hailed the biggest foreign investment deal in Russian history on Friday, when he took part in the signing ceremony of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC).
Nemtsov said the oil pipeline, with initial costs pegged at at $2 billion, will earn Russia a massive $23 billion over the expected 40-year life of the project.
"This is the biggest investment project in Russian history," he told reporters after the official signing ceremony.
"The project is of the utmost importance to Russia. It will bring $23 billion to Russia, or over 10 times the total outstanding debt to pensioners," he said.

CPC is an international consortium comprising eight companies and three governments. It will build a 1,500-km (940 mile) pipeline linking massive oil reserves in western Kazakhstan to Russia's Black Sea oil port of Novorossiisk.
Jeet Bindra, president of Chevron Pipe Line Co, said he expected the line to be completed by September 1999, and oil to flow shortly thereafter.
The consortium envisages transporting 28 million tonnes (560,000 barrels per day) in the early stages, building volumes gradually to 67 million (1.34 million bpd) by 2012 to 2014.
The agreement signed on Friday will allow full financing of the project to proceed and construction to begin, CPC said.
But officials added that the consortium still needed to complete feasibility studies, environmental reports and rights of way agreements before it could dig ditches and lay pipes.
"We are aiming at construction starting at the start of 1998," Bindra said.

Consortium members said that Nemtsov, who is also First Deputy Prime Minister and a rising star in President Boris Yeltsin's reformist cabinet, played a key role in pushing the deal through a myriad of bureaucratic traps.
"He personally was very instrumental in getting the decrees signed that were necessary," said Richard Matzke, president of Chevron Overseas Petroleum Inc.
Chevron Corp of the U.S. has a 15 percent stake in CPC, and is the largest single shareholder among the companies.
Nemtsov in turn handed the praise to his President.
"Only the intervention of Boris Yeltsin allowed this deal to get through the bureacracy," Nemtsov said. "It was only a month ago that today's signing was in grave doubt."

Attracting foreign investment to Russia's ailing oil industry has proved painfully slow since reforms began in the early 1990s. Friday's glittering ceremony only reinforced the impression that personalities still count in getting deals done.
Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have proved more successful in the energy sector, having signed multi-billion-dollar on- and offshore projects with international oil majors already.
Kazakhstan stands to earn $8.2 billion from the CPC project, CPC officials said.
"This is a great event which takes place today in Moscow. It paves the way for the practical implementation of the CPC," Kazakh Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin said in Almaty.
While the CPC does not involve oil production on Russian soil, Russia is set to earn huge transport fees.
Its largest oil company, LUKoil LKOH.RTS, has a 12.5 percent stake and state oil company Rosneft a 7.5 percent share.
The Russian government also owns 24 percent of the consortium, and may divide its share equally between LUKoil, Rosneft and Transneft, the oil pipeline monopoly.
The longer term knock-on effects could also be enormous.
Nemtsov said the CPC pipeline could be a way of introducing competition to the oil transport monopoly in Russia, forcing tariffs, which are a major part of oil firms' costs, lower.
It could also prove the catalyst to other international energy investment programmes Russia needs to reverse the steep decline in oil production and free up its oil export bottleneck.
"I think this will serve as a catalyst," Matzke said. "There was a feeling that if the CPC can't make it, we can't either."

CPC's shareholders, except Chevron, LUKoil and Rosneft, are Mobil Corp with 7.5 percent, Britain's BG Plc (formerly British Gas) and Italy's Agip SpA (two percent each), and Oryx Energy Company and Kazakhstan's Munaigaz (1.75 percent each).
The remaining 50 percent is divided between Russia (24 percent), Kazakhstan (19 percent) and Oman (seven percent).
